hints: Each edge can connect two consecutive vertices in a path cover; the graph is a DAG, so these links cannot create a cycle.
Create a bipartite graph with a left and right copy of every node, and add a bipartite edge for each original directed edge.
A maximum matching gives the fewest vertex-disjoint paths: the count is n minus the matching size. Reconstruct paths from nodes with no matched predecessor.
analogy: Match each path node to its next node; every successful match saves one path start.
example: In the first sample, choose matches 1?2 and 4?5. The resulting paths are 1,2 and 3,4,5, so the two paths cover every node exactly once.
algorithm: Run Hopcroft?Karp on the bipartite graph whose left and right sides are copies of the n DAG nodes and whose edges are (u_left,v_right) for every directed edge u?v. A matching of size M defines successor links: each matched u?v makes v the next node after u. If n-M>2, print NO. Otherwise start at every node with no matched predecessor and follow successor links to output each path; if there is only one path, output an empty second path. Print YES and the two node counts and lists.
correctness: A path cover with p paths uses exactly n-p links between consecutive path vertices, and those links form a matching because each vertex has at most one predecessor and successor. Thus any cover by at most two paths implies a matching of size at least n-2. Conversely, a matching creates disjoint successor chains; because the original graph is acyclic, these chains cannot form cycles, and they cover all vertices in n-M paths. Therefore a cover by at most two paths exists exactly when the maximum matching has size at least n-2, and reconstruction produces a valid cover.
complexity: O((n+m)?n) time with Hopcroft?Karp and O(n+m) space, where n is the number of nodes and m the number of directed edges.
